title: Tsakiroglou & Co. Ltd. v. Noblee Thorl G.m.b.H.
lead: Closure of Suez left a longer, more expensive route for groundnuts, but that change did not frustrate this c.i.f. sale or trigger its shipment exception.

actors.name: Tsakiroglou & Co. Ltd.
actors.role: Sellers who refused shipment after Suez closed

actors.name: Noblee Thorl G.m.b.H.
actors.role: Hamburg buyers seeking performance and damages

actors.name: Oil Seed Association tribunals
actors.role: Arbitrator and appeal board deciding the contractual dispute

proceedings: Arbitration and association appeal board: £5,625 damages award sustained on stated facts.
Diplock J. and Court of Appeal: upheld award.
House of Lords: unanimously dismissed appeal and preserved award and costs.
limits: The report year is 1962 but decision date is March 28, 1961. The court decided this sales contract, reserving different carriage obligations and extreme cost cases. Source is the complete reproduced report, not a recovered original reporter scan.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The sellers promise shipment during two months without specifying Suez
sections.cue: Introduce the sale before the route closes.
paragraphs: On October 4, 1956, Tsakiroglou agreed to sell Noblee Thorl about 300 tons of Sudanese groundnuts in shell, including bags, at £50 per 1,000 kilos, cost, insurance, and freight to Hamburg. Shipment was due in November or December. Ninety-five percent of the provisional invoice was payable against documents, with the rest after analysis and final invoice.

The Oil Seed Association form supplied London arbitration. Although it referred to a West African shipment port, the stated case found the parties intended Port Sudan, appropriate for these nuts. No express term required Suez. Sellers had the goods in Port Sudan warehouses from November 1 and booked vessels scheduled during the shipment period.

The canal closed November 2 and remained blocked until April 1957. Bookings were canceled November 4. A Cape of Good Hope route remained possible, about 11,137 rather than 4,386 miles. Freight initially about £7 10s. per ton carried a twenty-five-percent surcharge from November 10 and a one-hundred-percent surcharge from December 13. Sellers shipped nothing and treated the bargain as canceled.

sections.title: The commercial tribunals award damages and state the legal question
sections.cue: Trace the appeal and contractual exception.
paragraphs: An arbitrator awarded buyers £5,625 plus £79 15s. award costs. The association appeal board upheld it and stated a special case, finding Cape carriage possible and performance not commercially or fundamentally different. Diplock J. and the Court of Appeal upheld the award. Sellers argued in the House of Lords for an implied route term, frustration, and clause 6 force majeure.

They maintained that the ordinary route contemplated at formation defined performance and could not be replaced by an obligation that would previously have departed from the contract. Buyers answered that c.i.f. duties required reasonable carriage and proper documents assessed when shipment fell due, and increased expense did not change the sale’s essential character.

Clause 6 extended shipment or delivery by up to two months for specified events or force majeure preventing performance, then canceled for continuing impediment. All five Law Lords found it inapplicable. Closing Suez prevented that route, not bringing goods to the agreed port and loading for Hamburg by an available route. Their conclusion concerned this clause, not every force-majeure provision whenever any imaginable route exists.

sections.title: Simonds and Reid focus on the bargain’s obligations at performance
sections.cue: Explain why route construction and frustration remain separate.
paragraphs: Viscount Simonds declined to imply Suez exclusivity or an unqualified duty to use the formation-date customary route. Either could make buyers forgo goods after closure without contractual support. Custom was assessed when performance was due; absent a customary route, reasonable carriage was required with regard to goods and circumstances under the Sale of Goods Act.

Construction and frustration remained distinct: impossibility of one supposed term did not necessarily end the whole contract, and lack of such a term did not foreclose frustration. This was a goods sale with carriage only one element. No evidence showed deterioration, loss of a seasonal market, or breach of a material arrival requirement. Extra freight and insurance or lost profit did not fundamentally change it. Simonds rejected the contrary approach in the comparable Carapanayoti case.

Lord Reid likewise asked how rights and obligations after closure differed from performance through Suez, considering buyers too because frustration operated automatically and a falling market could make them invoke it. There was no demonstrated goods injury or buyer loss from transit time. Sellers procured carriage, bills of lading, and documents; they were not themselves undertaking the carrier’s voyage. They did not rely on this freight increase alone as sufficient, so Reid reserved astronomical expense and expressed no view on frustration of a separate shipowner’s contract.

sections.title: The other speeches find the alternative commercially reasonable
sections.cue: Preserve their distinct emphases and the law-fact boundary.
paragraphs: Lord Radcliffe treated usual practice as filling contractual gaps with reasonable mercantile performance, not freezing an unavailable route. The two-month window, varied vessel speeds, no required arrival date, and no proof of deterioration or special packing supported Cape carriage. His blocked-front-door analogy illustrated reasonable substitution, not an unconditional duty to accept any expense or risk.

Lord Hodson also relied on reasonable carriage and no Suez-only term. A vital arrival date or inability of the goods to survive might matter, but neither appeared. Freight remained a component of price, and sellers principally challenged the longer voyage’s character rather than expense alone. Lord Guest judged carriage at shipment time and distinguished an unavailable contemplated method from a radically different obligation frustrating the entire bargain.

All five rejected treating the appeal board’s broad no-fundamental-difference statement as conclusive on law. Arbitrators properly found cost, time, risk, and condition; the combined legal consequence remained judicial. Simonds treated commercial assessment as valuable evidence, Reid separated specific facts from ultimate inference, and Radcliffe cautioned against a rigid mercantile law-fact divide while preferring detailed findings to a summary. Hodson and Guest likewise respected commercial assessment without surrendering the legal question.

sections.title: The existing award remains payable to the buyers
sections.cue: Finish with the formal order and contract-specific limits.
paragraphs: On March 28, 1961, Viscount Simonds and Lords Reid, Radcliffe, Hodson, and Guest each voted to dismiss, unanimously affirming the Court of Appeal. The formal order directed payment of the £5,625 deposited in court to the buyers and required sellers to pay appellate costs. There was no new damages trial.

The result addressed a seller’s c.i.f. undertaking, not every separate carrier contract affected by the same closure. Physical disruption had to be measured against this contract’s obligations and commercial consequences. The later 1962 reporter date does not change the 1961 decision date.
